video_title: Lawfare Daily: Dispatches from the 2026 Aspen Security Forum
gist: Four attendees of the July 14-17, 2026 Aspen Security Forum (Mark Leon Goldberg, Cory Shaki, Alex Zerden, Alexandra Bell) report that the dominant storyline was a closed Strait of Hormuz and an Iran war widely judged a disaster, with the on-stage establishment consensus still prescribing more military pressure. The most investable threads are Zerden's warning that the buffers holding oil prices down (Chinese demand destruction and reserve draws) are nearing exhaustion, his skepticism that USTR Greer's assumption of an indestructible US consumer holds, the post-Supreme Court pivot from IEEPA tariffs to Sections 301/232, and a stranded-fertilizer food-price shock rippling through the Horn of Africa. The Trump administration sent almost no security officials, leaving the forum dominated by private sector, civil society, foreign governments, and retired officials.

themes.theme: Hormuz Closure and the Iran Quagmire

insights.claim: At the 2026 Aspen Security Forum's opening panel, Conda Rice, Ambassador Nick Burns, Penny Pritsker and former Defense Secretary Mark Esper converged on the view that the US cannot let Iran control the Strait of Hormuz, and the only prescription offered was more military pressure, with no pushback until Senator Chris Murphy took the stage later.
insights.speaker: Mark Leon Goldberg
insights.so_what: The US foreign policy establishment's revealed preference is escalation rather than a negotiated reopening, so investors should not price in a near-term diplomatic de-escalation of the Hormuz shipping disruption.
insights.quote: is it really like the state of quote you know establishment thought right now that the straight of Hormuz can be opened through the application of military force

insights.claim: Mark Leon Goldberg's takeaway from Aspen is that there is no solution to the Hormuz crisis and the strait will remain closed for the foreseeable future, because the military pressure now being advertised as the fix is what closed it in the first place.
insights.speaker: Mark Leon Goldberg
insights.so_what: A prolonged Hormuz closure is a persistent tail risk for energy, tanker rates, marine insurance and fertilizer/food supply chains rather than a transitory headline event.
insights.quote: there is no solution to the hormuz crisis and you know uh that you know it will remain closed for the foreseeable future

insights.claim: Goldberg offers a recurring quagmire framework from 20 years covering Iraq and Afghanistan: when a policy is failing, policymakers' knee-jerk impulse is to escalate rather than exit, drawing the country deeper into uncertain outcomes, and Iran is the latest instance.
insights.speaker: Mark Leon Goldberg
insights.so_what: A reusable base rate for handicapping US conflict paths: default expectation should be gradual escalation and duration extension, not resolution, which favors longer-dated risk premia in energy and defense.
insights.quote: there is always a consistent line of thought that compels policymakers to want to throw more resources at a failing problem

insights.claim: Cory Shaki argues the 2025 Iran war had a clear objective largely fulfilled by the 12-day war, while the 2026 choices made by Israel and the United States were much sloppier, under-resourced and not thought through, a distinction she says was missing from Aspen's blanket consensus that the whole undertaking was a disaster.
insights.speaker: Cory Shaki
insights.so_what: If the failure is specific to 2026 execution rather than the entire campaign, the policy correction (and any de-escalation trade) hinges on 2026 decision-makers, not a wholesale reversal of the Iran strategy.
insights.quote: the choices that both Israel and the United States made in 2026, which I think were much sloppier, much less well resourced, and very clearly not thought through

insights.claim: Alex Zerden reports that former Defense Secretary Mark Esper told the Aspen audience, in Zerden's paraphrase, that economic tools are effectively the only options left against Iran because military options have not succeeded to date, and that sanctions are being reinjected into both the Iran and Russia conversations.
insights.speaker: Alex Zerden
insights.so_what: Expect the next phase of Iran and Russia policy to be sanctions-led, raising compliance, secondary-sanctions and payment-rail risk for firms with Gulf, Russian or crypto exposure.
insights.quote: the economic options are really the only options left to challenge and contest Iran, that the military options have not succeeded to date

insights.claim: Alexandra Bell warns that Iran hovered at breakout capability for years without deciding to build a weapon, that the US does not know where all the fissile material is (something the Trump administration's own intelligence community has alluded to), and that the strikes may have pushed Tehran into finally deciding it needs a nuclear capacity, which short of a ground invasion and occupation could not be stopped.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Bell
insights.so_what: A weaponization decision by Iran would reprice regional escalation risk, Gulf security guarantees and proliferation cascades far beyond the current Hormuz disruption.
insights.quote: did we push the Iranian regime into into finally deciding that yes, they do need a nuclear capacity

insights.claim: Cory Shaki, who holds the Kissinger chair at the Library of Congress and is writing a book on why the United States cannot win wars, concluded from the Aspen panels that the Trump administration has not found a new American way of war but only new ways to lose American wars.
insights.speaker: Cory Shaki
insights.so_what: A credibility-erosion thesis from an AEI defense-policy lead signals that allied hedging and adversary risk-taking are likely to increase, a slow-burn negative for US-anchored security assumptions.
insights.quote: the Trump administration hasn't found a new American way of war. They've just found new ways to lose American wars.

themes.theme: Oil, Food and the Exhausting Buffers

insights.claim: Oil has stayed within a relatively stable price band since the Iran war began, with no $200 barrels, because Chinese demand destruction and reserve draws absorbed the shock, but Alex Zerden says the sidebar consensus at Aspen is that this resiliency is nearing its end and major price spikes in oil and other products transiting Hormuz are a real risk factor.
insights.speaker: Alex Zerden
insights.so_what: The single most tradeable claim in the episode: the buffer that has kept crude range-bound is depleting, arguing for upside convexity in energy and for hedging refined-product and freight exposure.
insights.quote: We haven't gotten $200 barrels of oil as a result of the war

insights.claim: Zerden says China presents an opaque or incomplete picture of its oil reserves and reserve capabilities, that there is consensus the reserves have decreased, and that despite years of nuclear reactor buildout and its position as a huge producer and consumer of solar and other renewables, China remains heavily reliant on imported oil.
insights.speaker: Alex Zerden
insights.so_what: Chinese reserve depth is the key unknown determining how long global crude stays capped; watch Chinese import and stockpile data as the leading indicator for the next leg in oil.
insights.quote: How how deep are their reserves? That's the live question.

insights.claim: Goldberg identifies a second-order food shock from the Hormuz closure: fertilizer that the Horn of Africa depends on has been stranded on the wrong side of the strait through an entire planting season, so global food prices that are already high are poised to go much higher with destabilizing knock-on effects.
insights.speaker: Mark Leon Goldberg
insights.so_what: A missed planting season creates a lagged, hard-to-reverse agricultural supply shortfall, arguing for exposure to fertilizer and soft commodities and for political-instability risk in import-dependent frontier markets.
insights.quote: fertilizer that they normally depend on that transits the straight of horm has been stuck on the wrong side through the course of an entire planting season

insights.claim: Zerden frames the current environment as 'permacrisis' - a sequence of COVID supply-chain and public-health shocks, the Russia-Ukraine disruption to oil, gas and fertilizer molecules with downstream food-production effects on poor countries, and now the Iran war - and argues it is a management problem that will never be solved rather than a crisis to be resolved.
insights.speaker: Alex Zerden
insights.so_what: Treats disruption as a permanent operating regime, favoring companies and portfolios built for resilience and optionality over those priced on mean-reverting stability.
insights.quote: It's it's a management problem. It's not going to be solved ever.

themes.theme: Tariff Authorities After the IEEPA Ruling

insights.claim: Following a Supreme Court decision nullifying the use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act for certain tariff measures, US Trade Representative Jameson Greer told Aspen he is optimistic about the administration's remaining authorities under Section 301 and Section 232 and other ways to deploy tariffs.
insights.speaker: Alex Zerden
insights.so_what: The tariff regime is being re-plumbed rather than dismantled, so importers should model Section 301/232 sector- and country-specific actions rather than assume broad tariff relief from the court ruling.
insights.quote: ambassador Greer seems optimistic about the their authorities under section 301, section 232

insights.claim: Alex Zerden flags that Jameson Greer's trade framework treats the resilience of the US consumer as a constant, and argues it is better understood as a variable given recent inflation numbers, supply-chain shocks and potential AI displacement of the labor force.
insights.speaker: Alex Zerden
insights.so_what: The core assumption underpinning aggressive tariff policy is consumer absorption capacity; if consumption cracks under inflation or AI-driven job displacement, tariff policy and consumer-exposed equities both reprice.
insights.quote: he has a lot of confidence in the certainty of the resilience of the US consumer

insights.claim: Greer used his Aspen remarks to plant a flag about Chinese supply chain vulnerabilities without elaborating, which Zerden called an interesting nugget and speculated may be intimating China's own oil dependence.
insights.speaker: Alex Zerden
insights.so_what: A hint that Washington is preparing to press Chinese supply-chain and energy-import vulnerabilities rather than only defend US ones, which would open a new front in the trade conflict.
insights.quote: there are Chinese supply chain concerns that exist and he didn't go into too much detail about it

themes.theme: Nuclear Risk and Hollowed-Out Arms Control

insights.claim: Alexandra Bell, formerly at the State Department, says the president fired all of the State Department staff working on multilateral nuclear arms control despite repeatedly saying he wants to reduce nuclear threats, and that she is not even sure trained nuclear experts are in the ongoing Iran dialogues because the administration is not transparent about who attends.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Bell
insights.so_what: Loss of technical negotiating capacity lowers the probability of any verifiable Iran or Russia nuclear deal, extending the geopolitical risk premium rather than resolving it.
insights.quote: he fired all of the people at the State Department working on multilateral nuclear arms control

insights.claim: Bell characterizes the present as the most dangerous nuclear situation since the end of the Cold War with everything in the nuclear space trending in the wrong direction, yet says nuclear issues received minimal treatment at the Aspen Security Forum and were touched only briefly when Iran or Russia came up.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Bell
insights.so_what: A risk the policy community itself is under-discussing is by definition under-priced by markets, making nuclear escalation an unhedged tail.
insights.quote: Everything in the nuclear space is trending in the wrong direction.

insights.claim: Bell notes that China is rapidly expanding its nuclear arsenal in an opaque and dangerous fashion while refusing strategic stability dialogues and intimidating regional neighbors, and yet Europeans now view China more favorably than before, which she calls a reality check on how much trust the United States has lost.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Bell
insights.so_what: European sentiment drifting toward China despite Chinese nuclear expansion signals durable transatlantic realignment risk for supply chains, export controls and alliance-dependent trades.
insights.quote: it's also surprising to me that that people would give trust to a country that's given them no reason to trust them

insights.claim: Bell reports that climate change never came up at the 2026 Aspen Security Forum and biological risks did not come up once despite the world being less than five years past the most disruptive biological event in a hundred years, though one panel did cover the security implications of AI.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Bell
insights.so_what: Attention has rotated wholesale from climate and pandemic risk to AI and kinetic conflict, a sentiment shift that affects where security-adjacent policy money and mandates flow next.
insights.quote: I haven't heard biological risks come up at all.

insights.claim: The Trump administration sent no Department of Defense representatives and only limited participation overall to the 2026 Aspen Security Forum, with Ambassador Greer among the few attendees, in contrast to Biden-era forums that drew the CIA director, National Security Adviser Sullivan and the secretary of state.
insights.speaker: Alex Zerden
insights.so_what: Reduced official participation lowers the informational value of these forums as a read on actual US policy, forcing analysts to rely more on formal announcements and less on off-record signaling.
insights.quote: no representatives uh from the department of defense

insights.claim: Goldberg traces the drop-off to last year, when the defense secretary barred military officials from attending at the last minute with a knock-on chilling effect on other administration officials, and notes the administration did the same to the Halifax International Security Conference held in Canada each November.
insights.speaker: Mark Leon Goldberg
insights.so_what: A systematic policy of disengagement from Western security conferences, not a one-off, so expect thinner official signal from Halifax and similar venues going forward.

insights.claim: Cory Shaki attributes the absence of US security officials to unwillingness to hear about the disappointment their policies are fostering and to the MAGA wing's resentment of elite consensus-building forums, while noting that a notable number of retired military officers and retired national security career officials showed up to sustain the policy dialogue.
insights.speaker: Cory Shaki
insights.so_what: The formal policy channel and the expert channel are decoupling, meaning expert consensus is a weaker predictor of actual US action than in prior administrations.
insights.quote: this is a security forum and there was nobody from the security departments of the United States government. And I think it's because they don't want to hear the disappointment and the challenges that their policies are fostering.

insights.claim: Zerden argues from experience inside the administration that governing burns down intellectual capital every day through the tyranny of the inbox, so outside interaction with civil society and academia - even bad ideas - improves policy, and that low administration turnout shifted this year's Aspen composition toward the private sector, civil society, foreign governments and journalists as speakers rather than moderators.
insights.speaker: Alex Zerden
insights.so_what: Policy quality degrades when the outside-expertise loop is cut, raising the odds of unforced errors and abrupt policy reversals that markets have to absorb without warning.
insights.quote: you're burning down your intellectual capital every day. Uh just the process of governing, the tyranny of the inbox

themes.theme: Bipartisanship, Norms and US Legal Legitimacy

insights.claim: A forum attendee highlighted Carl Rove's on-stage rejection of Vice President Vance's blood-and-soil approach to American citizenship and his argument that this is not the most dangerous time in American politics, citing earlier eras that were more violent and contested, calling the message weirdly comforting and hopeful about the political system's tools to handle contestation.
insights.speaker: forum attendee
insights.so_what: Evidence of an intra-Republican split on nationalism and a case that US institutional resilience is being underrated, relevant to how much political-risk discount to apply to US assets.
insights.quote: Carl Rove was guns blazing with his rejection of Vice President Vance's blood and soil approach to American citizenship

insights.claim: Alexandra Bell criticizes a reticence at Aspen to name the real problems - lip service to bipartisan solutions without discussing actual solutions, and tiptoeing around the administration's undermining of democratic principles and of international structures the US spent decades building in its own national security and economic interest.
insights.speaker: Alexandra Bell
insights.so_what: If the expert community self-censors on institutional erosion, public discourse will lag the actual deterioration, meaning institutional risk gets recognized late and repriced abruptly.
insights.quote: We can pay lip service to, you know, bipartisan solutions, but we actually have to talk about the solutions

insights.claim: A Lawfare-affiliated participant argues the missing layer at Aspen was legal: US moves to undermine bodies like the International Criminal Court and to cast aside international legal norms when they are inconvenient, combined with domestic legal turmoil, erode the image of a fair and just society and hand Russia and China the argument that the US is just like them.
insights.speaker: Lawfare-affiliated participant
insights.so_what: Legitimacy erosion is a compounding cost to US soft power and coalition-building capacity, weakening the enforceability of sanctions and export-control regimes that depend on allied cooperation.
insights.quote: the US isn't actually what it says it is. They're just like us.

insights.claim: Goldberg identifies Sudan as the largest humanitarian crisis in the world today, with the Rapid Support Forces militia massing outside the city of El Oed and poised to sack it, and notes that in every city the militia has taken over three years of conflict it has committed mass atrocities, making this a looming mass atrocity event.
insights.speaker: Mark Leon Goldberg
insights.so_what: A near-term, forecastable atrocity event with sanctions and diplomatic-crisis potential that is currently absent from the security-forum agenda and therefore from market attention.
insights.quote: there is a genocidal militia called the rapid support forces which is massing outside of city a city called El Oed

insights.claim: Goldberg says Sudan's civil war is to a large degree fueled and funded by outside powers - the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and Saudi Arabia - giving it an international security dimension that connects it directly to the Gulf conversations happening at Aspen.
insights.speaker: Mark Leon Goldberg
insights.so_what: Gulf state sponsorship makes Sudan a potential sanctions and reputational flashpoint for UAE, Egyptian and Saudi counterparties, not merely a humanitarian story.

insights.claim: Goldberg reports Myanmar's civil war passed a grim milestone of 100,000 conflict-related deaths earlier this month, making it by far the deadliest conflict in Asia, and that China recently entered the conflict in a more decisive way with unclear objectives and unclear consequences for its relations with India.
insights.speaker: Mark Leon Goldberg
insights.so_what: Direct Chinese intervention on the Myanmar border is a geopolitical development with China-India implications that is being ignored by the foreign policy establishment and therefore not priced.
insights.quote: passed a grim milestone of 100,000 conflict related deaths earlier this month. By far the deadliest conflict in Asia.

insights.claim: Zerden says the largest bank robbery in the world occurred last year without breaking into popular consciousness: North Korean actors hacked a cryptocurrency exchange in the UAE, and the proceeds are funding both North Korea's and Russia's war machines, while North Korea itself remains an evergreen existential threat to South Korea and Japan that nobody can build a conference panel around.
insights.speaker: Alex Zerden
insights.so_what: State-scale crypto theft is now a sanctions-evasion and war-financing channel, raising custody, exchange-security and AML risk for digital-asset venues, especially in the Gulf.
insights.quote: they hacked into a cryptocurrency exchange in the UAE and it's funding their war machine, it's funding Russia's war machine

insights.claim: Zerden argues overseas scam centers running romance and confidence schemes at hypercharged scale using digital assets are stealing Americans' entire life savings, driving bankruptcies, mortgages taken against savings and 401(k) draws, that the administration has taken some reasonable steps against it, and that this cross-cutting multi-jurisdictional issue deserves far more attention at forums like Aspen.
insights.speaker: Alex Zerden
insights.so_what: Household-level crypto fraud losses are a rising regulatory catalyst; expect more enforcement and compliance obligations on payment rails and digital-asset intermediaries.
insights.quote: stealing people's entire life savings making people go bankrupt having people take out mortgages

themes.theme: Pakistan and Turkey as Swing Middle Powers

insights.claim: Zerden says Pakistan surfaced at Aspen as a key node and interlocutor in the US-Iran negotiations, with some of the talks having occurred in Pakistan, while simultaneously carrying unresolved issues from its most recent war with India, exposure through Pakistani migrant workers in the Gulf hit by the Iran war, a strategic-depth security umbrella it provides to certain Gulf states, and its own status as a nuclear power.
insights.speaker: Alex Zerden
insights.so_what: Pakistan is an under-watched single point of failure connecting the Iran negotiation track, Gulf security guarantees and South Asian nuclear escalation risk.

insights.claim: Zerden flags Turkey as the other middle power that surfaced on the Aspen sidelines: active in the US-Iran war dynamics, in tension with Israel including a contest between the two in Syria, expanding its role in Africa, and, though a NATO ally, taking steps after a recent summit that may concern US policymakers and complicate implementation of existing sanctions regimes.
insights.speaker: Alex Zerden
insights.so_what: Turkey's divergence from US positions inside NATO creates sanctions-enforcement gaps and a live Israel-Turkey contest in Syria that could become the next regional escalation vector.
insights.quote: they're NATO NATO ally but coming even coming out of the Ankor summit you know doing some things that may be concerning to US policy makers
